comparisons.peer_summary: Citi considers opportunities to redeem or repurchase long-term debt to reduce funding costs, having redeemed or repurchased an aggregate of $46.8 billion of outstanding long-term debt during 2024.
comparisons.comparison: Both BAC and Citi disclose active strategies to manage long-term debt liabilities through repurchases or redemptions. BAC states it may purchase outstanding debt instruments depending on market conditions and liquidity, while Citi explicitly mentions considering opportunities to redeem or repurchase long-term debt to reduce funding costs. A key difference is in the reported outcome for 2024: Citi quantified its activity by stating it redeemed or repurchased an aggregate of $46.8 billion of outstanding long-term debt, whereas BAC's disclosure focuses on the strategic capability and net decrease in total debt driven by maturities and redemptions ($18.9 billion decrease) without explicitly aggregating the buyback/repurchase volume in the same sentence.

sentences.text: Total long-term debt decreased $18.9 billion to $283.3 billion during 2024, primarily due to maturities and redemptions, partially offset by debt issuances and valuation adjustments.
We may, from time to time, purchase outstanding debt instruments in various transactions, depending on market conditions, liquidity and other factors.

As part of its liability management, Citi has considered, and may continue to consider, opportunities to redeem or repurchase its long-term debt pursuant to open market purchases, tender offers or other means.
During 2024, Citi redeemed or repurchased an aggregate of $46.8 billion of its outstanding long-term debt.

comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures discuss the drivers of changes in long-term debt/borrowings, specifically highlighting the interplay between new issuances and existing debt obligations (maturities/redemptions). BAC reports a net decrease in long-term debt of $18.9 billion primarily due to maturities and redemptions, partially offset by issuances. In contrast, Morgan Stanley reports a net increase in total borrowings to $289 billion, primarily driven by issuances exceeding maturities and redemptions. Both companies reference specific mechanisms for determining maturity profiles, with BAC mentioning the general nature of debt instruments and MS providing specific definitions for original maturity based on contractual dates or put options.
